pages.title: Trading Analytics
pages.description: Trading analytics helps traders review trade history, expectancy, win rate, profit factor, drawdown, risk per trade, holding time, and performance behaviour with clearer data.
pages.keywords: trading analytics, trading performance analytics, trading analytics platform, trade analytics, trading performance analysis, trader analytics, trading statistics, Turtle Analytics
pages.intro: Trading analytics turns trade history into evidence. Green Turtle Trades gives traders a clearer way to understand performance by connecting account history, journal records, risk metrics, and Turtle Analytics dashboards.

sections.title: What trading analytics means
sections.body: Trading analytics is the process of reviewing trade history, risk, return, timing, behaviour, and consistency to understand how a trader is actually performing. It should explain the pattern behind the results rather than only showing an account balance.

sections.title: Different from a journal or tracker
sections.body: A trading journal records decisions, notes, and lessons. A performance tracker summarizes results. Trading analytics goes further by connecting those records to deeper metrics, behaviour patterns, risk quality, and possible areas for improvement.

sections.title: Performance data built around real trading history
sections.body: Good trading analytics should explain what is happening across actual trades, not rely on screenshots or headline returns. Turtle Analytics reviews recorded trade history so traders can understand where performance is strong, where risk is too high, and which behaviours need attention.

sections.title: Core analytics metrics
sections.body: Useful trading analytics include expectancy, win rate, R-multiple, profit factor, average win, average loss, risk/reward, risk per trade, drawdown, holding time, trade count, best trade, worst trade, sample size, and consistency.

sections.title: Risk-adjusted performance
sections.body: Raw P/L can be misleading if it was produced by oversized positions, high leverage, or a single outlier trade. Green Turtle Trades reviews performance alongside drawdown, open exposure, stop-loss behaviour, leverage where available, and risk consistency.

sections.title: Data sources for analytics
sections.body: Turtle Analytics can support analytics workflows from journal records, platform activity, MetaTrader-connected MT4 and MT5 history, Trading 212 history, and CSV imports where available. Public summaries should always make the data source and calculation method clear.

sections.title: Realised and unrealised performance
sections.body: Analytics should distinguish realised performance from closed trades and unrealised performance from open positions. That separation helps prevent confusion between completed results and live exposure.

sections.title: Private analytics, optional public summaries
sections.body: Raw trade data, account details, and notes remain private by default. Traders can choose to publish controlled summary performance where supported, while public metrics should follow methodology-backed calculations.

sections.title: Trading analytics for evaluation
sections.body: Green Turtle Trades uses analytics to support clearer trader evaluation. Verified summaries, competition rankings, and future trader-backed investing workflows should be based on structured performance evidence rather than unsupported claims.

faqs.question: What is trading analytics?
faqs.answer: Trading analytics is the process of reviewing trade history, risk, return, expectancy, win rate, drawdown, timing, and behaviour patterns to understand trading performance.

faqs.question: How is trading analytics different from a trading journal?
faqs.answer: A trading journal records decisions, notes, and lessons. Trading analytics turns those records into metrics and patterns such as expectancy, drawdown, profit factor, and risk behaviour.

faqs.question: Which trading analytics metrics matter most?
faqs.answer: Useful metrics include expectancy, win rate, R-multiple, profit factor, average win, average loss, risk per trade, drawdown, holding time, sample size, and consistency.

faqs.question: Can Turtle Analytics use MT4 or MT5 history?
faqs.answer: Turtle Analytics supports MetaTrader-connected workflows for MT4 and MT5 traders, alongside Trading 212 history and CSV import workflows where available.

faqs.question: Does Turtle Analytics predict market prices?
faqs.answer: No. Turtle Analytics focuses on historical trade behaviour and performance analysis. It does not make market predictions or guarantee returns.

faqs.question: Should analytics include open positions?
faqs.answer: Open positions can be included when reviewing full account exposure, but unrealised performance should be labelled separately from realised closed-trade performance.

faqs.question: Can CSV trades be used in private analytics?
faqs.answer: Yes. CSV trades can be used privately for analytics and journal work, but CSV-imported trades are excluded from public leaderboard calculations.

pages.intro: Trading education should help traders understand their own decisions, risk, and performance quality. Green Turtle Trades groups its practical guides around trading journals, analytics, risk metrics, performance statistics, trader verification, and the university investment competition.

sections.title: Start with the trading journal
sections.body: A trading journal is the base layer. It records entries, exits, notes, lessons, risk, holding time, setups, and market context so traders can review decisions as well as outcomes.

sections.title: Turn records into analytics
sections.body: Trading analytics turns journal and account history into metrics such as win rate, average return, profit factor, expectancy, drawdown, risk per trade, holding time, trade count, and consistency.

sections.title: Understand expectancy
sections.body: Expectancy helps traders understand the average expected outcome of a trade by combining win rate, average win, average loss, and sample size. It is often more useful than win rate alone.

sections.title: Understand drawdown
sections.body: Drawdown explains downside risk. It measures how far an account falls from a previous equity high and helps traders judge the risk behind a return figure.

sections.title: Review profit factor and risk/reward
sections.body: Profit factor compares gross winning outcomes with gross losing outcomes. Risk/reward compares the amount risked with the expected or realised reward. Both metrics help explain payoff quality.

sections.title: Keep risk management central
sections.body: Risk management is not separate from performance. Traders should review risk per trade, open exposure, leverage where available, stop-loss behaviour, largest loss, drawdown, and consistency.

sections.title: Understand trader verification
sections.body: Trader verification should make performance harder to misunderstand. Good verification labels data sources, separates public summaries from private raw records, and makes calculation limits clear.

sections.title: Learn through the university competition
sections.body: The Green Turtle Trades University Investment Competition gives Scottish students a risk-free environment to learn practical investing, portfolio discipline, risk control, and transparent performance review.

faqs.question: What should new traders learn first?
faqs.answer: New traders should start with journaling, risk per trade, drawdown, win rate, expectancy, and the difference between realised and unrealised performance.

faqs.question: Which trading metrics matter most?
faqs.answer: Useful metrics include expectancy, win rate, profit factor, average win, average loss, risk/reward, drawdown, risk per trade, holding time, sample size, and consistency.

faqs.question: Why is trading education linked to analytics?
faqs.answer: Analytics helps traders see whether their decisions are producing repeatable results or whether performance is being driven by outliers, weak risk control, or small sample size.

faqs.question: Does trading education guarantee better returns?
faqs.answer: No. Trading education can improve understanding and review discipline, but it does not guarantee future returns or remove market risk.

faqs.question: How does Green Turtle Trades use education in the university competition?
faqs.answer: The competition gives students virtual capital and public rankings so they can learn practical investing, risk control, and performance review without risking personal money.

pages.title: Trading Journal
pages.description: A trading journal for recording trades, reviewing decisions, importing MT4 and MT5 history, tracking lessons, measuring expectancy, and understanding trading risk.
pages.keywords: trading journal, trade journal, trading journal software, trading journal app, MT4 trading journal, MT5 trading journal, trading performance journal, trade notes, trading analytics journal
pages.intro: A trading journal is where traders turn trade history into feedback. Green Turtle Trades helps traders keep a structured record of entries, exits, notes, lessons, risk, account activity, and performance metrics so each trade becomes part of a clearer review process.

sections.title: What a trading journal should record
sections.body: A useful trading journal should hold more than entry and exit prices. Traders should be able to review the symbol, direction, size, entry, exit, stop loss, take profit, risk, holding time, order type, setup, notes, lessons learned, and the market context around the decision.

sections.title: Why spreadsheets and screenshots are weak
sections.body: Spreadsheets can be useful at the start, but they often become hard to maintain and easy to misread. Screenshots are even weaker because they can be selective and rarely show risk, sizing, context, or the full account history. A structured journal keeps the record more consistent.

sections.title: Review decisions as well as outcomes
sections.body: The point of a trading journal is not just to see whether a trade made money. It should help traders understand whether the trade followed the plan, whether risk was controlled, whether the exit was disciplined, and whether the same mistake keeps appearing over time.

sections.title: Build a review process
sections.body: A journal is most useful when traders review it regularly. Weekly and monthly reviews can show which setups are working, which symbols create avoidable losses, whether risk is drifting, and whether trades are being taken for clear reasons or emotional reactions.

sections.title: Connect journal data to Turtle Analytics
sections.body: Green Turtle Trades connects journal records with Turtle Analytics so traders can move from simple record keeping to deeper performance analysis across expectancy, profit factor, win rate, drawdown, holding time, R-multiple, best and worst trades, and risk behaviour.

sections.title: Import MT4, MT5, Trading 212, and CSV history
sections.body: A journal becomes more useful when trade history can be imported rather than manually rebuilt from memory. Turtle Analytics supports MetaTrader-connected workflows for MT4 and MT5 traders, Trading 212 history, and CSV imports where available, then brings that history into one structured review process.

sections.title: Measure expectancy and trading quality
sections.body: Journal metrics should show whether the trading process has a positive expected outcome. Expectancy, average win, average loss, win rate, risk/reward, profit factor, and average return help traders understand whether performance is repeatable or dependent on isolated trades.

sections.title: Separate realised and unrealised performance
sections.body: Closed trades and open positions should not be mixed without labels. Realised performance comes from closed trades, while unrealised performance depends on open positions and current market marks. Clear labels help prevent account numbers from drifting across different screens.

sections.title: Track risk, drawdown, and exposure
sections.body: Green Turtle Trades treats risk as part of the journal, not a separate afterthought. Traders can review drawdown, risk per trade, open exposure, leverage where available, largest loss, missing stop-loss behaviour, and consistency signals across their own trading history.

sections.title: Private records, optional public summaries
sections.body: Journal data stays private by default. Raw trades, notes, account details, and personal records should not be exposed publicly. Traders may choose to publish controlled summary metrics, but public performance should be clearly labelled and methodology-backed.

sections.title: Built for beginners and serious traders
sections.body: Beginners can use a journal to build discipline and stop repeating avoidable mistakes. More experienced traders can use it to test whether a strategy is producing a real edge, whether risk is consistent, and whether behaviour changes across market conditions.

sections.title: A private record that can support public proof
sections.body: The private journal is for honest review. If a trader later chooses to publish a performance summary, the public version should use controlled metrics, clear data-source labels, and methodology-backed calculations rather than exposing private notes or unsupported claims.

faqs.question: What should a trading journal include?
faqs.answer: A trading journal should include entry and exit data, symbol, direction, position size, stop loss, take profit, risk, holding time, notes, trade lessons, market context, and performance metrics.

faqs.question: Is a trading journal better than a spreadsheet?
faqs.answer: A spreadsheet can work for simple tracking, but a structured trading journal is better for combining notes, risk, imported history, review workflows, and analytics in one place.

faqs.question: Is a trading journal useful for beginners?
faqs.answer: Yes. A journal helps new traders build discipline, review mistakes, and understand whether progress is based on repeatable behaviour.

faqs.question: Can a trading journal connect to MT4 or MT5?
faqs.answer: Turtle Analytics supports MetaTrader-connected workflows for MT4 and MT5 traders, alongside Trading 212 history and CSV import workflows where available.

faqs.question: Which trading journal metrics matter most?
faqs.answer: Useful journal metrics include expectancy, win rate, profit factor, average win, average loss, risk/reward, drawdown, risk per trade, holding time, and trade count.

faqs.question: Does a trading journal predict future trades?
faqs.answer: No. A trading journal reviews historical decisions and outcomes. It can help traders identify patterns and risks, but it does not predict market prices or guarantee returns.

faqs.question: Should a trading journal include open positions?
faqs.answer: Open positions can be included, but unrealised performance should be labelled separately from realised closed-trade performance.

faqs.question: Are my journal trades public?
faqs.answer: No. Raw journal trades, notes, and account details stay private by default. Only controlled summary stats can appear publicly if a trader enables public performance features.

pages.intro: Verification means checking a trading record against stated evidence and reviewing risk in context. It supports GTT's proposed professional client service, but does not guarantee selection or future returns. Virtual competition records are identified separately.

sections.title: Why verified trader records matter
sections.body: A trader's headline return is not enough. A useful verification workflow should help explain whether results came from repeatable behaviour, responsible risk, a meaningful trade sample, and real trading history rather than edited screenshots or unsupported claims.

sections.title: Screenshots are not verification
sections.body: Screenshots can be cropped, selective, edited, or disconnected from the wider account history. Green Turtle Trades treats screenshots as weak evidence compared with structured platform records, connected account data, imported broker history, MetaTrader-connected data, or in-house competition executions.

sections.title: What verification means
sections.body: Verification means a trading record is supported by platform-recorded activity, connected account data, imported broker history, MetaTrader-connected history, or in-house competition execution records. It does not mean Green Turtle Trades guarantees future performance or labels any trader as risk-free.

sections.title: Data source labels
sections.body: Verified summaries should make the data source clear. Public pages should distinguish between in-house competition data, connected account data, imported broker history, MetaTrader-connected records, journal records, and private analytics imports.

sections.title: Risk-adjusted performance, not only P/L
sections.body: Trader evaluation should look beyond profit and loss. Green Turtle Trades focuses on metrics such as win rate, expectancy, drawdown, profit factor, risk per trade, average hold time, open exposure, sample size, and consistency so users can understand the shape of performance.

sections.title: Realised and unrealised performance
sections.body: Verified performance should label realised and unrealised values separately. Realised performance comes from closed trades. Unrealised performance depends on open positions and current market marks. Keeping those numbers distinct makes public summaries easier to trust.

sections.title: Duplicate and incomplete records
sections.body: Good verification should handle duplicate trades, missing identifiers, incomplete exits, stale market marks, and mismatched account totals. The goal is to avoid counting the same trade twice or mixing incompatible data sources.

sections.title: Performance without exposing raw trades
sections.body: Public trader profiles should show controlled summary performance while keeping raw trades, account details, private notes, and personal information protected. This gives visitors a clearer view of trader quality without exposing sensitive trading records.

sections.title: Useful public summary metrics
sections.body: A useful public trader summary can include total return, realised return, unrealised return, win rate, average return, drawdown, profit factor, expectancy, risk label, trade count, active positions, and sample-size warnings where needed.

sections.title: Connected to methodology
sections.body: The Green Turtle Trades methodology explains how data sources, realised and unrealised P/L, risk labels, duplicate trade handling, public summaries, and competition calculations should be treated. Verified trader pages should stay aligned with that methodology.

sections.title: Review for professional client accounts
sections.body: The proposed investment service considers verified live records alongside strategy review and the regulated host's assessment. A public profile or competition ranking alone is not approval for client money.

sections.title: Limits of verification
sections.body: Verification does not remove trading risk. Historical performance can change, data can be incomplete, open positions can move quickly, and market conditions can shift. Public trader data is informational and should not be treated as financial advice.

faqs.question: What is a verified trader?
faqs.answer: A verified trader is a trader whose performance can be reviewed through platform-recorded activity, connected account data, imported broker history, MetaTrader-connected records, or in-house competition execution data rather than unsupported claims alone.

faqs.question: Are trading screenshots enough to verify a trader?
faqs.answer: No. Screenshots can be selective or missing context. Verification is stronger when it uses structured records, connected account data, imported broker history, or platform-recorded executions.

faqs.question: Does verified mean risk-free?
faqs.answer: No. Verified means the record is supported by a data source. It does not mean future performance is guaranteed or that the trader is risk-free.

faqs.question: Do verified traders publish every raw trade?
faqs.answer: No. Raw trades, account details, and private notes stay private by default. Public pages should show controlled summary statistics such as return, win rate, expectancy, risk, drawdown, and trade count.

faqs.question: Which metrics matter for trader verification?
faqs.answer: Useful verification metrics include realised and unrealised return, win rate, expectancy, profit factor, drawdown, risk per trade, average hold time, sample size, exposure, and consistency.

faqs.question: Why are CSV trades excluded from public ranking?
faqs.answer: CSV files can be edited outside the platform, so they are not trusted for public leaderboard ranking calculations.

faqs.question: What is the difference between public summaries and raw trades?
faqs.answer: Public summaries show controlled metrics such as return, win rate, risk, drawdown, and trade count. Raw trades, account details, and private journal notes remain private by default.

faqs.question: Are verified trader summaries financial advice?
faqs.answer: No. Public rankings, verified summaries, and trader analytics are informational and should not be treated as financial advice or guarantees of future results.

pages.keywords: trading performance tracker, trading performance, trade tracker, trading metrics, track trading performance, trading statistics, trading dashboard, trader performance analytics
pages.intro: A trading performance tracker helps traders understand whether their results are consistent, risk-aware, and repeatable. Green Turtle Trades combines performance tracking with journal records, account history, risk analytics, and Turtle Analytics dashboards.

sections.title: What a trading performance tracker does
sections.body: A trading performance tracker records and summarizes trading results so traders can review the full pattern behind their trades. It should show more than account balance by connecting trade outcomes, risk, timing, notes, and behaviour.

sections.title: Track the metrics that explain performance
sections.body: Win rate, expectancy, R-multiple, profit factor, average win, average loss, risk/reward, risk per trade, drawdown, holding time, trade count, best trade, worst trade, and sample size all help explain whether trading results come from a repeatable edge.

sections.title: Sample size and consistency matter
sections.body: A small number of winning trades can create misleading confidence. A useful performance tracker should help traders judge whether results are backed by enough trades, whether wins and losses are consistent, and whether one outlier trade is doing too much of the work.

sections.title: Connect results to behaviour
sections.body: Performance tracking is most useful when it links results to trader behaviour, notes, timing, market conditions, setup quality, and risk decisions. Green Turtle Trades connects tracking with journal records so traders can review both the result and the decision process.

sections.title: Track realised and unrealised performance clearly
sections.body: Performance pages should distinguish realised P/L from closed trades and unrealised P/L from open positions. Total performance is clearer when the source of each figure is labelled and calculated consistently.

sections.title: Use one calculation source
sections.body: A tracker becomes unreliable if the dashboard, journal, leaderboard, and admin tools all recalculate numbers differently. pages.title: Trading Risk Management
pages.description: Trading risk management tools and analytics for reviewing risk per trade, drawdown, exposure, stop-loss behaviour, leverage, expectancy, and trader consistency.

pages.intro: Risk management is central to serious trading. Green Turtle Trades helps traders review risk per trade, drawdown behaviour, open exposure, stop-loss discipline, leverage where available, expectancy, and performance consistency.

sections.title: Risk is part of every trade
sections.body: Every trade has risk. The question is whether that risk is measured, controlled, and consistent with the trader's edge, account size, and trading plan. A trader can have strong returns and still be fragile if the risk behind those returns is uncontrolled.

sections.title: Risk per trade
sections.body: Risk per trade shows how much of the account is exposed if a trade fails. Where a stop loss is available, risk can be estimated from the distance between entry and stop multiplied by size. Where stop data is missing, Green Turtle competition risk logic uses conservative fallback signals such as notional exposure and leverage.

sections.title: Drawdown and largest loss
sections.body: Drawdown shows how far performance falls from a previous equity high. Largest loss shows how much damage one trade created. Together, they help traders understand whether returns are being earned with acceptable downside or with hidden blow-up risk.

sections.title: Stop-loss behaviour and risk/reward
sections.body: A risk workflow should show whether trades have planned exits, whether stop-loss behaviour is consistent, and whether average reward is large enough compared with average risk. Win rate alone is not enough without understanding risk/reward.

sections.title: Open exposure and leverage
sections.body: Risk does not only exist in closed trades. Open exposure, correlated positions, leverage where available, and concentrated symbols can all increase account vulnerability. Turtle Analytics helps traders review exposure alongside realised performance.

sections.title: Competition risk score inputs
sections.body: The competition risk score blends average risk per trade, missing stop-loss rate, average leverage, largest loss percentage, and open exposure percentage. Lower risk scores receive better risk labels, while limited samples may be marked provisional or unrated.

sections.title: Use analytics to spot weak risk habits
sections.body: Trading analytics can highlight oversized risk, weak setups, poor reward-to-risk behaviour, overtrading, long hold times, missing stop-loss patterns, and conditions where a trader tends to underperform.

sections.title: Risk-adjusted trader evaluation
sections.body: Green Turtle Trades treats risk as part of performance quality. Verified summaries, trader comparisons, and competition scoring should consider return alongside drawdown, sample size, exposure, and risk consistency rather than rewarding raw P/L alone.

sections.title: Public rankings reward controlled risk
sections.body: Public rankings and competition scoring should reward controlled risk because responsible risk control supports more sustainable performance. Risk labels are summary indicators, not financial advice or guarantees of future returns.

faqs.question: What is trading risk management?
faqs.answer: Trading risk management is the process of controlling position size, risk per trade, drawdown, exposure, stop-loss behaviour, leverage, and decision quality across trades.

faqs.question: Why is risk per trade important?
faqs.answer: Risk per trade shows how much a trader is exposing on each position. Consistent risk helps make performance easier to evaluate.

faqs.question: What is trading drawdown?
faqs.answer: Drawdown measures how far an account or strategy falls from a previous equity high to a later low. It helps show downside risk behind the returns.

faqs.question: Why is risk/reward important?
faqs.answer: Risk/reward compares how much a trader risks against the potential or realised reward. A high win rate can still be weak if losses are much larger than wins.

faqs.question: Should open positions be included in risk review?
faqs.answer: Yes. Open positions affect exposure, unrealised P/L, leverage, and concentration risk, so they should be reviewed alongside closed-trade performance.

faqs.question: Can analytics improve trading risk management?
faqs.answer: Analytics can reveal patterns in losses, drawdowns, trade duration, stop placement, exposure, oversized trades, and conditions where risk tends to increase.

faqs.question: Are risk labels investment advice?
faqs.answer: No. Risk labels and analytics are informational summaries. They are not financial advice and do not guarantee future performance.

pages.title: Trading Expectancy
pages.description: Trading expectancy explained: formula, examples, win rate, average win, average loss, risk/reward, sample size, and how Turtle Analytics reviews expectancy.
pages.keywords: trading expectancy, expectancy trading, trading expectancy formula, trade expectancy, expectancy calculator trading, win rate risk reward, trading metrics
pages.intro: Trading expectancy helps traders understand the average expected outcome of a trade over a series of trades. It connects win rate, average win, average loss, risk/reward, and sample size into one practical performance metric.

sections.title: What trading expectancy means
sections.body: Trading expectancy estimates the average result a trader can expect per trade based on historical outcomes. It is useful because it looks beyond whether a trader wins often and asks whether the size of wins is large enough compared with the size of losses.

sections.title: Trading expectancy formula
sections.body: A common formula is: expectancy = (win rate x average win) - (loss rate x average loss). For example, if a trader wins 50% of trades, averages £120 on winners, and loses £70 on losers, expectancy is (0.50 x 120) - (0.50 x 70) = £25 per trade.

sections.title: Why win rate alone is not enough
sections.body: A trader can have a high win rate and still lose money if losses are much larger than wins. A trader can also have a lower win rate and still be profitable if average wins are meaningfully larger than average losses.

sections.title: Expectancy and risk/reward
sections.body: Expectancy connects directly to risk/reward. When a trader risks £100 to make £50, the win rate needs to be much higher than when a trader risks £100 to make £200. The relationship between win rate and average win/loss size is what expectancy makes visible.

sections.title: Expectancy needs sample size
sections.body: Expectancy is more useful when it is based on enough trades. A small sample can be distorted by one large win or loss, while a larger sample gives a clearer view of whether the trading process has a repeatable edge.

sections.title: Account expectancy and R-multiple expectancy
sections.body: Expectancy can be reviewed in currency terms, percentage terms, or R-multiple terms. R-multiple expectancy can be helpful because it normalizes outcomes by the amount risked on each trade.

sections.title: Expectancy calculator example
sections.body: If a trader wins 50% of trades, averages £120 on winners, and loses £70 on losers, expectancy is (0.50 x £120) - (0.50 x £70), which equals £25 per trade before costs and future market changes.

sections.title: Expectancy in the competition scoring model
sections.body: In the competition scoring model, expectancy is reviewed as average R-multiple from closed competition trades where risk can be estimated. It contributes to trade quality, but it does not override return, drawdown, risk control, consistency, or participation.

sections.title: How Turtle Analytics uses expectancy
sections.body: Turtle Analytics connects expectancy with journal records, trade history, risk per trade, drawdown, holding time, and setup behaviour. That helps traders see whether expectancy is coming from disciplined repeatable decisions or from isolated outlier trades.

sections.title: Limitations of expectancy
sections.body: Expectancy is based on historical data. It does not predict future trades, remove market risk, or guarantee returns. It should be reviewed alongside drawdown, exposure, sample size, and risk consistency.

faqs.question: What is trading expectancy?
faqs.answer: Trading expectancy is the average expected outcome per trade based on win rate, average win, loss rate, and average loss.

faqs.question: What is the trading expectancy formula?
faqs.answer: A common formula is expectancy = (win rate x average win) - (loss rate x average loss).

faqs.question: Can a trader be profitable with a low win rate?
faqs.answer: Yes. A trader can be profitable with a lower win rate if average wins are large enough compared with average losses.

faqs.question: Why is expectancy better than win rate alone?
faqs.answer: Win rate only shows how often trades win. Expectancy also considers the size of wins and losses, which gives a clearer view of performance quality.

faqs.question: Does positive expectancy guarantee future returns?
faqs.answer: No. Positive historical expectancy does not guarantee future results. Market conditions, risk behaviour, sample size, and execution can all change.

faqs.question: How does Turtle Analytics review expectancy?
faqs.answer: Turtle Analytics reviews expectancy alongside trade history, journal records, risk per trade, drawdown, holding time, and other performance metrics.

pages.title: Trading Drawdown
pages.description: Trading drawdown explained: max drawdown, equity high to low, realised and unrealised drawdown, recovery math, risk control, and how Turtle Analytics reviews drawdown.
pages.keywords: trading drawdown, max drawdown trading, maximum drawdown, drawdown meaning trading, drawdown calculator trading, equity drawdown, trading risk management
pages.intro: Trading drawdown shows how far an account, strategy, or trader falls from a previous equity high. It is one of the most important risk metrics because it reveals the downside behind a return figure.

sections.title: What trading drawdown means
sections.body: Drawdown measures the fall from a previous equity peak to a later low. If an account rises to £110,000 and then falls to £100,000 before recovering, the drawdown from that peak is £10,000 or about 9.09%.

sections.title: Maximum drawdown
sections.body: Maximum drawdown is the largest peak-to-trough fall in the period being reviewed. It helps traders and evaluators understand the worst historical downside in a trading record.

sections.title: Drawdown is different from one losing trade
sections.body: A single losing trade can contribute to drawdown, but drawdown measures the account-level decline across a sequence of trades or open positions. It captures the combined effect of losses, exposure, and unrecovered equity.

sections.title: Realised and unrealised drawdown
sections.body: Realised drawdown comes from closed losses and account history. Unrealised drawdown can come from open positions moving against the trader. A full risk review should make clear whether drawdown includes open trade marks or only closed performance.

sections.title: Why drawdown matters more than headline return
sections.body: Two traders can both make 10%, but one may have experienced a 2% drawdown while another went through a 25% drawdown. The return number alone does not show how much downside risk was taken to reach it.

sections.title: Recovery math
sections.body: The deeper a drawdown becomes, the larger the return needed to recover. A 10% drawdown needs about 11.1% to recover, while a 50% drawdown needs 100% to recover. This is why controlling downside matters.

sections.title: Drawdown recovery table
sections.body: Approximate recovery requirements are: 5% drawdown needs 5.3% recovery, 10% needs 11.1%, 20% needs 25.0%, 30% needs 42.9%, 40% needs 66.7%, and 50% needs 100.0%.

sections.title: How competition drawdown is measured
sections.body: Competition drawdown is calculated from the account equity path in chronological order. Closed trades move the realised equity curve, and unrealised P/L from open positions can also affect drawdown when the page represents full account performance.

sections.title: How Turtle Analytics reviews drawdown
sections.body: Turtle Analytics reviews drawdown alongside trade history, risk per trade, open exposure, leverage where available, holding time, expectancy, and journal records. That helps traders see whether drawdown came from normal strategy variance or weak risk behaviour.

sections.title: Limitations of drawdown
sections.body: Drawdown is based on available historical data. It does not predict the next loss, remove trading risk, or guarantee that future drawdown will be smaller. It should be reviewed with sample size, exposure, risk consistency, and market context.

faqs.question: What is drawdown in trading?
faqs.answer: Drawdown in trading is the decline from a previous account or strategy equity high to a later low.

faqs.question: What is maximum drawdown?
faqs.answer: Maximum drawdown is the largest peak-to-trough decline over the period being measured.

faqs.question: Why is drawdown important?
faqs.answer: Drawdown shows the downside risk behind returns. It helps traders understand how much equity was lost before recovery.

faqs.question: Is drawdown the same as a loss?
faqs.answer: No. A loss is usually a single trade or realised outcome. Drawdown measures the wider equity decline from a previous high.

faqs.question: Should open positions count toward drawdown?
faqs.answer: Open positions can affect unrealised drawdown. Pages should label whether drawdown includes open trade marks or only closed-trade performance.

faqs.question: Does low drawdown guarantee a safe trader?
faqs.answer: No. Low historical drawdown does not guarantee future safety. Drawdown should be reviewed alongside exposure, sample size, leverage, risk per trade, and market conditions.

pages.title: Profit Factor in Trading
pages.description: Profit factor in trading explained: formula, gross profit, gross loss, sample size, win rate, expectancy, drawdown, and how Turtle Analytics reviews profit factor.
pages.keywords: profit factor trading, trading profit factor, profit factor formula, good profit factor trading, gross profit gross loss, trading metrics, Turtle Analytics
pages.intro: Profit factor shows how much gross profit a trader generated for every unit of gross loss. It is a useful trading metric because it connects winning trades and losing trades into one simple ratio, but it needs sample size and risk context to be meaningful.

sections.title: What profit factor means
sections.body: Profit factor compares total profits from winning trades with total losses from losing trades. A profit factor above 1.0 means gross profits were larger than gross losses over the period being reviewed. A profit factor below 1.0 means losses were larger than profits.

sections.title: Profit factor formula
sections.body: The common formula is: profit factor = gross profit / absolute gross loss. For example, if a trader made $1,500 from winning trades and lost $750 from losing trades, the profit factor is 2.0.

sections.title: Why gross profit and gross loss matter
sections.body: Profit factor uses gross totals rather than net profit alone. That matters because two traders can have the same net profit but very different risk profiles. One may have smooth gains and controlled losses, while another may swing through large wins and large losses.

sections.title: What is a good profit factor?
sections.body: A profit factor above 1.0 is positive historically, but it does not automatically mean the strategy is strong. A very high profit factor can be distorted by a small trade sample, one large outlier, or a period with no meaningful losses.

sections.title: Profit factor needs sample size
sections.body: Profit factor is more useful when there are enough closed trades. With only a few trades, the ratio can move sharply after one win or one loss. Sample size, trade count, and consistency should always be reviewed alongside profit factor.

sections.title: Profit factor vs win rate
sections.body: Win rate shows how often trades win. Profit factor shows whether the wins were large enough compared with the losses. A trader can have a lower win rate and a strong profit factor if average wins are much larger than average losses.

sections.title: Profit factor vs expectancy
sections.body: Expectancy estimates the average outcome per trade. Profit factor compares total winning output with total losing output. Both metrics are useful, but expectancy is usually better for understanding the average trade and profit factor is useful for understanding aggregate payoff quality.

sections.title: How Turtle Analytics reviews profit factor
sections.body: Turtle Analytics reviews profit factor alongside win rate, average win, average loss, expectancy, drawdown, holding time, risk per trade, and sample size. In the journal workflow, profit factor is calculated from winning outcomes divided by the absolute value of losing outcomes when enough loss data exists.

sections.title: Limitations of profit factor
sections.body: Profit factor is based on historical results. It does not predict future trades, remove market risk, or guarantee future performance. It should be read with drawdown, exposure, trade count, and risk consistency.

faqs.question: What is profit factor in trading?
faqs.answer: Profit factor is the ratio of gross profit from winning trades to the absolute gross loss from losing trades.

faqs.question: What is the profit factor formula?
faqs.answer: The common formula is profit factor = gross profit / absolute gross loss.

faqs.question: What is a good profit factor?
faqs.answer: A profit factor above 1.0 is historically positive, but it should be reviewed with sample size, drawdown, risk, and consistency.

faqs.question: Can profit factor be misleading?
faqs.answer: Yes. Profit factor can be misleading when it is based on very few trades, one large outlier, or a period with no meaningful losses.

faqs.question: Is profit factor better than win rate?
faqs.answer: Profit factor shows whether wins were large enough compared with losses, while win rate only shows how often trades won. Both should be reviewed together.

faqs.question: Does high profit factor guarantee future returns?
faqs.answer: No. High historical profit factor does not guarantee future returns. Market conditions, risk behaviour, and execution can all change.

pages.title: Risk/Reward Ratio in Trading
pages.description: Risk/reward ratio in trading explained: planned risk, potential reward, realised average win/loss, win rate, expectancy, and how Turtle Analytics reviews risk/reward.
pages.keywords: risk reward ratio trading, risk/reward trading, trading risk reward ratio, reward risk ratio, win rate risk reward, trading expectancy
pages.intro: Risk/reward ratio compares how much a trader is risking with how much they are trying to make. It is one of the most practical trading metrics because it shows why win rate alone is never enough.

sections.title: What risk/reward ratio means
sections.body: Risk/reward ratio compares planned downside with planned upside. If a trader risks $100 to target $200, the planned reward is twice the planned risk, often described as 2:1.

sections.title: Risk/reward formula
sections.body: A common formula is: risk/reward = potential reward / amount risked. The same idea can also be reviewed after trades close by comparing average winning trade size with average losing trade size.

sections.title: Planned ratio vs realised ratio
sections.body: Planned risk/reward uses the stop-loss, entry, and take-profit idea before the trade. Realised risk/reward uses what actually happened after trades closed. Both are useful, but realised average win/loss behaviour is often more reliable than what a trader intended.

sections.title: Why win rate and risk/reward belong together
sections.body: A trader with a 40% win rate can still be profitable if average wins are much larger than average losses. A trader with an 80% win rate can still lose money if losses are very large. Risk/reward explains the trade-off.

sections.title: Risk/reward and expectancy
sections.body: Expectancy combines win rate and average win/loss size into one average expected outcome. Risk/reward is one of the main inputs that makes expectancy positive or negative over a series of trades.

sections.title: Average win/loss ratio
sections.body: When stop-loss and take-profit data is incomplete, platforms can still review realised payoff quality by comparing average winner size with average loser size. This is often displayed as an average win/loss or payoff ratio.

sections.title: Risk/reward and discipline
sections.body: A good planned ratio only matters if trades are executed consistently. Moving stops, closing winners early, adding to losers, or oversizing positions can make the realised ratio weaker than the planned setup.

sections.title: How Turtle Analytics reviews risk/reward
sections.body: Turtle Analytics reviews risk/reward alongside expectancy, profit factor, drawdown, average win, average loss, risk per trade, holding time, and journal notes. Where full plan data is unavailable, realised average win/loss behaviour helps show the actual payoff profile.

sections.title: Limitations of risk/reward
sections.body: Risk/reward does not guarantee profitability. It must be read with win rate, execution quality, sample size, slippage, market conditions, and whether trades followed the original plan.

faqs.question: What is risk/reward ratio in trading?
faqs.answer: Risk/reward ratio compares the amount a trader risks with the amount they are trying to make on a trade.

faqs.question: How do you calculate risk/reward ratio?
faqs.answer: A common calculation is potential reward divided by amount risked. For closed trades, traders can also review average win size divided by average loss size.

faqs.question: Is 2:1 risk/reward always good?
faqs.answer: No. A 2:1 setup still depends on win rate, execution quality, costs, slippage, and whether the trader follows the plan.

faqs.question: Can a low risk/reward strategy be profitable?
faqs.answer: Yes. A lower risk/reward strategy can be profitable if the win rate is high enough and losses are controlled.

faqs.question: Is risk/reward the same as profit factor?
faqs.answer: No. Risk/reward compares risk and reward per trade or average trade. Profit factor compares total gross profit with total gross loss.

faqs.question: Does risk/reward guarantee returns?
faqs.answer: No. Risk/reward is a planning and review metric. It does not guarantee future returns or remove market risk.

pages.title: Trader Verification Guide
pages.description: Trader verification guide explaining verified trading records, data sources, screenshots, public summaries, private raw data, risk metrics, and Green Turtle Trades methodology.

pages.intro: Trader verification should make performance harder to misunderstand. A strong verification workflow explains where the data came from, which metrics were calculated, what is public, what stays private, and what the limits of the record are.

sections.title: Why trader verification matters
sections.body: Trading performance is easy to exaggerate when it is shown through screenshots, edited spreadsheets, or isolated wins. Verification creates a more structured record so traders, evaluators, and investors can review performance with clearer evidence.

sections.title: Screenshots are not enough
sections.body: Screenshots can be cropped, selective, or missing context. A useful verification process should rely on platform-recorded activity, connected account data, imported history, or in-house execution records where possible.

sections.title: What verified can mean
sections.body: Verified does not mean risk-free. It means a trading record is supported by a stated data source. That source might be platform-recorded competition executions, connected broker history, MetaTrader history, uploaded records, or journal data depending on the product area.

sections.title: Data source labels
sections.body: Public pages should label whether data is live platform data, imported broker history, MetaTrader-connected history, journal records, or competition execution data. Clear labels reduce confusion and help users understand the strength of the evidence.

sections.title: Private raw data vs public summaries
sections.body: Raw trades, account details, and private journal notes should not automatically be public. Public profiles can show controlled summaries such as return, win rate, profit factor, expectancy, drawdown, risk labels, and trade count while keeping sensitive records private.

sections.title: Metrics that matter
sections.body: Useful verification metrics include realised return, unrealised return, total return, win rate, expectancy, profit factor, drawdown, risk per trade, average hold time, sample size, exposure, and consistency.

sections.title: Handling duplicate or weak data
sections.body: Verification should be strict about duplicate trades, missing identifiers, stale marks, incomplete exits, and mismatched account totals. The same account should use one central calculation source so public pages, app screens, and admin screens do not drift apart.

sections.title: How Green Turtle Trades approaches verification
sections.body: Green Turtle Trades separates raw records from public summaries, uses central metric logic where possible, and explains calculation rules in the trader verification methodology. The aim is clear evidence, not unsupported performance claims.

sections.title: Limits of verification
sections.body: Verification does not guarantee future performance, remove trading risk, or mean a trader is suitable for every investor. Public analytics and rankings are informational and should not be treated as financial advice.

faqs.question: What is trader verification?
faqs.answer: Trader verification is the process of supporting a trading record with clear data sources, calculation rules, and controlled performance summaries.

faqs.question: Why are screenshots not enough to verify a trader?
faqs.answer: Screenshots can be selective or missing context. Verification is stronger when it uses platform-recorded activity, connected account data, or imported account history.

faqs.question: Does verified mean a trader is safe?
faqs.answer: No. Verified means the record is supported by stated data. It does not mean the trader is risk-free or guaranteed to perform in the future.

faqs.question: Do verified traders need to publish raw trades?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Public profiles can show controlled summary metrics while raw trades, account details, and private journal notes remain private.

faqs.question: Which metrics matter for trader verification?
faqs.answer: Important metrics include realised and unrealised return, win rate, expectancy, profit factor, drawdown, risk per trade, average hold time, trade count, sample size, exposure, and consistency.

sections.title: Public and private information
sections.body: Raw trade history, account details, personal information, and private journal notes should remain private unless a user or competition rule explicitly makes a summary public. Public pages should use summary statistics such as score, return, win rate, risk label, trade count, university ranking, and competition activity rather than exposing sensitive account data.

sections.title: Core performance metrics
sections.body: Common metrics include realised return, unrealised return, total return, win rate, average return, profit factor, expectancy, drawdown, holding time, trade count, and risk score. Metrics should be calculated from the relevant backend account or competition dataset rather than being manually re-entered or recalculated differently in the frontend.

sections.title: Return and P/L treatment
sections.body: Realised P/L should come from closed trades. Unrealised P/L should come from open positions using the latest available market mark. Total P/L combines realised and unrealised values where appropriate. If a page is based only on closed journal trades, it should be labelled as realised or journal-based rather than presented as full account P/L.

sections.title: Competition account projection
sections.body: For competition accounts, starting balance is the account starting balance, realised P/L is the sum of deduped closed-trade P/L, unrealised P/L is the sum of open-position P/L, total P/L is realised plus unrealised, equity is starting balance plus total P/L, and return percentage is total P/L divided by starting balance.

sections.title: Win rate and trade count
sections.body: Competition trade count is based on closed competition trades after duplicate handling. Win rate is calculated from non-zero closed trades only: winning non-zero closed trades divided by all non-zero closed trades. Zero-P/L closed trades can count toward closed-trade sample size but do not distort win-rate percentage.

sections.title: Profit factor and expectancy
sections.body: Profit factor is gross profit divided by absolute gross loss. Competition expectancy is based on average R-multiple where risk can be estimated, while the broader analytics pages may also discuss currency or percentage expectancy for journal review.

sections.title: Risk and drawdown
sections.body: Risk analysis should consider drawdown, average risk per trade, leverage where available, missing stop-loss behaviour, open exposure, largest loss, and concentration. Drawdown should measure the fall from a previous equity high to a later low in the relevant dataset. Risk labels are summary indicators, not investment recommendations.

sections.title: Risk score formula inputs
sections.body: The competition risk score blends average risk per trade, missing stop-loss rate, average leverage, largest loss percentage, and open exposure percentage. The label is Unrated when there is no activity, Low for lower risk scores, Medium for mid-range scores, and High for elevated scores, with provisional labels where sample size is limited.

sections.title: University competition calculations
sections.body: University competition rankings use in-house competition data and central scoring logic. Individual scores, university scores, active participation, realised and unrealised return, backers, risk labels, and trade activity should come from the central competition calculation source so public pages, the app, and admin views do not drift apart.

sections.title: Individual competition score inputs
sections.body: Individual competition scoring blends total return quality, trade quality from expectancy and win rate, participation, risk control, drawdown control, and consistency. Penalties apply for no market activity, negative return, drawdown above 15%, and high risk score.

sections.title: Data quality and duplication controls
sections.body: Where trade records can arrive from more than one source, calculations should avoid counting duplicate executions as separate trades. Trade matching should use stable close-order identifiers where available and fall back to consistent fingerprints based on symbol, direction, P/L, return percentage, holding time, and exit date.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.body: Verification and analytics depend on the available data. Missing broker fields, delayed market prices, imported file errors, duplicated records, timezone differences, and open positions can affect reported metrics. Green Turtle Trades should label data sources and update methodology notes when calculation rules materially change.

sections.title: Methodology version
sections.body: This methodology is a public summary for Green Turtle Trades website and competition reporting. Methodology version 1.0 was published in August 2026 and should be reviewed whenever scoring, verification, data-source, or risk-calculation logic changes.

faqs.question: Does verified performance guarantee future returns?
faqs.answer: No. Verified performance means the record is supported by platform, account, import, or competition data. Historical performance does not guarantee future performance.

faqs.question: Does Green Turtle Trades publish raw account data?
faqs.answer: Public pages should use summary metrics and leaderboard information. Raw account details, personal information, and private journal notes should not be exposed publicly unless a specific product rule or user permission allows it.

faqs.question: How should realised and unrealised P/L be handled?
faqs.answer: Realised P/L comes from closed trades. Unrealised P/L comes from open positions using the latest available market mark. Total P/L combines them only when the page is representing full account performance.

faqs.question: How is competition win rate calculated?
faqs.answer: Competition win rate is calculated from non-zero closed trades: winning non-zero closed trades divided by all non-zero closed trades.

faqs.question: What inputs go into the competition risk score?
faqs.answer: The risk score blends average risk per trade, missing stop-loss rate, average leverage, largest loss percentage, and open exposure percentage.

faqs.question: Why does methodology matter for trader verification?
faqs.answer: A clear methodology helps users understand where the data comes from, what each metric means, and what limitations apply before comparing traders or competition results.

faqs.question: Are public rankings financial advice?
faqs.answer: No. Public rankings, analytics, trader summaries, and competition data are informational and should not be treated as financial advice or guarantees of future results.

sections.title: A risk-free way to learn practical investing
sections.body: An investment competition should reward process as well as outcome. Green Turtle Trades gives competitors virtual capital so they can learn position sizing, risk control, market behaviour, and portfolio discipline before real money is involved.

sections.title: Rankings based on more than return
sections.body: The competition leaderboard considers return, win rate, active participation, risk, drawdown, and trader-backing activity. This helps prevent pure high-risk speculation from dominating the ranking.

sections.body: Visitors can follow the public university competition leaderboard, compare top student traders, and see how universities rank against each other during the competition.

faqs.question: What is an investment competition?
faqs.answer: An investment competition is a structured challenge where competitors manage virtual or real capital and are ranked by performance, risk, activity, and other rules.

faqs.question: Does the Green Turtle Trades competition use real money?
faqs.answer: Competitors use virtual capital in the university competition, so students can gain practical experience without risking personal money.

faqs.question: How are competitors ranked?
faqs.answer: Competitors are ranked using a balanced scoring model covering return, win rate, participation, risk control, drawdown, and competition activity.
